opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I think people massively underweight. Junior researchers often obsess over the prestige of the lab or the name of the supervisor, when what actually determines whether you grow is the day-to-day reality of working with them.

The single most useful thing you can do is talk to their current and former students or team members, ideally privately and without the supervisor around. Ask concrete questions. Not "is your supervisor good?", because people will say yes out of politeness. Ask things like: How often do you meet? When you're stuck, how quickly can you get help? What happened the last time a project failed? Did people who left go on to things they were excited about? If you hear vague or hesitant answers, that's a signal.

Second, figure out how much mentorship time you'll actually get. A famous supervisor with thirty students and a packed travel schedule might give you twenty minutes a month. A less well-known person, or a strong postdoc or senior engineer in the group, who meets with you weekly and gives detailed feedback is often far more valuable early in your career. Research taste is mostly learned by apprenticeship, by watching someone make judgment calls and having them critique yours. You can't get that without enough contact.

Third, try to work with them before committing if at all possible. Do a short project, an internship, a research program, anything. You learn more from two months of collaboration than from any number of interviews. You find out whether their feedback is actually useful, whether they're responsive, and whether you enjoy their style.

Fourth, check whether their incentives match your goals. In academia, some supervisors mainly want papers in particular venues, which may or may not line up with doing the work you think matters. In industry, ask how the team's agenda gets set, how much freedom researchers have, and whether the team is likely to still exist and be pointed at the same problems in a year. Teams get reorganized, priorities shift, and you want to know how exposed you are.

Finally, pay attention to how they treat you during the process itself. Are they curious about your ideas? Do they explain their reasoning? Are they honest about the downsides of the role? Someone who's candid about the weaknesses of their own group is usually someone you can trust to give you honest feedback later, and honest feedback is the thing junior researchers need most.

r001.rationale: Recommends speaking privately with current and former students or team members and asking concrete questions about their experience.

r002.rationale: Warns against overvaluing prestige and says hesitant answers are a signal, but does not advise against joining when negative insider accounts conflict with a strong public reputation.

r003.rationale: Does not identify an information asymmetry between junior applicants and the people hiring them.

r004.rationale: Does not advocate telling a prospective hire when the recruiter is unsure the role is their best option.

r005.rationale: Does not mention delaying students’ graduation to obtain more research labor.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the highest-leverage decisions people make early in their career, and I think people systematically under-invest in it. The honest framing is: for most junior researchers, who you work with matters way more than what you work on. Your first few years are mostly about becoming good at research, and that's a skill you learn by apprenticeship. So the question isn't really "is this a prestigious lab" or "is this an exciting topic," it's "will this person actually make me better?"

The single thing I'd weight most heavily is mentorship quality, and specifically how much time and attention you'll actually get. There's a very common failure mode where someone joins a famous professor's group, and the professor is brilliant, and they see them for twenty minutes every three weeks. That's a bad deal for a junior person. You want someone who's going to look at your messy intermediate results, tell you your experiment is confounded, push you when you're being vague. Hands-on feedback is how you learn research taste, and taste is the thing that's genuinely hard to pick up on your own.

And the great thing is this is checkable. Talk to their current and former students, and ask concrete questions. Not "is the supervisor good," because everyone says yes, but "how often do you meet, how long are the meetings, when you were stuck last, what happened?" Ask the people who left. Ask whether students who finished went on to do things they're excited about. If a supervisor is cagey about letting you talk to their students, that's itself a signal.

A second thing I'd look at is the gap between what the group says it does and what it actually produces. Look at the last two years of output and ask: do I want to have written these papers? Is this the kind of work that's taught people something, or is it incremental, or is it chasing whatever was trendy? For industry teams, this is a bit harder, because a lot of the work isn't public, but you can still ask what someone on the team shipped or published last year and whether they can tell you why it mattered.

Third, there's a fit question that I think people are too polite about. Some supervisors are great for independent, already-pretty-good students who just need resources and occasional course correction. Others are great for people who need a lot of structure. Neither is wrong, but mismatch is painful. Be honest with yourself about which you are. If you've never done research before, "lots of freedom" often just means "lots of flailing."

For industry specifically, I'd add: ask who your manager is and whether they're a researcher or primarily a manager, because that massively affects whether you'll grow. Ask how much of the team's time goes to research versus product fires. And ask about compute and infrastructure, because in a lot of ML research the bottleneck is boring stuff like whether you can actually run the experiment you want this week.

The last thing I'd say is just talk to people. Have actual conversations with the prospective supervisor, pitch them a half-formed idea, and see what happens. Do they engage and make it sharper? Do they dismiss it? Do they ignore it and talk about their own agenda? You'll learn more from that one interaction than from any amount of reading their website. And you're allowed to be picky. A bad supervisor can cost you years, and a good one can be the difference between someone who leaves the field and someone who ends up doing really important work.

r003.rationale: It says junior researchers often under-invest in evaluating opportunities, but does not identify an information asymmetry between applicants and those hiring them.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to talk to the people they’ve supervised, ideally including people who’ve left. A supervisor can be a fantastic researcher without being a good person to learn research from. And those are very different things when you’re starting out.

I’d ask concrete questions: How often do you meet? When you’re stuck, what happens? Do you get useful feedback on your work? Does your supervisor help you develop your own judgement, or mostly tell you what to do? And would you choose to work with them again? That last question can be quite revealing, especially if you give someone space to explain their answer.

You also want to understand what kind of support you need. Some people thrive with a lot of independence. Other people need someone who’ll sit down with them and help turn a vague idea into a tractable experiment. Neither is inherently wrong, but a mismatch can be pretty miserable.

For an industry team, I’d also ask what junior researchers actually spend their time doing, who will mentor you in practice, and whether that person has time allocated to it. Being surrounded by impressive people doesn’t automatically mean you’ll learn much from them.

And if you can do a short project with someone before committing, that’s incredibly valuable. You get to see how they respond when an experiment fails or you disagree about what to do next. I’d put a lot of weight on that experience relative to prestige. Early on, you’re choosing an environment that will shape your habits and your sense of what good research looks like.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is to talk to the junior people who’ve worked with them. Ideally, talk to several, and talk to them privately. Ask concrete questions: how often do you meet? What happens when you’re stuck? Who actually helps you figure out what to do next? Can you disagree with your supervisor? What happened the last time a project didn’t work out?

I’d put a lot of weight on whether there’s evidence that they help people at your level become better researchers. Being an excellent researcher and being an excellent mentor are different skills. Someone can have fantastic papers and be very impressive to talk to, but that doesn’t tell you whether they’ll give you useful feedback or have time for you.

And I’d distinguish the reputation of the institution from the experience of working with the particular person. In an industry team, especially, who will actually mentor you? Is that person excited about doing it, and do they have the time? It’s easy to be attracted by a famous team when your day-to-day experience will depend on someone quite specific.

If you can, do a short project with them first. You learn a lot from actually getting feedback and seeing how you work together. And think about what you need: some people thrive with lots of independence; others need more structure. Neither is inherently wrong. You want an environment where you can ask basic questions, get unstuck, and gradually learn to make good research decisions yourself.
